p: Jordan Reyes has never flown anything.
Her older brother Danny died in March, at his daughter's soccer game.
For eleven years he flew a white 1978 Cessna called Biscuit out of Centennial Airport, south of Denver, and owned a quarter of her with three partners in a little flying club.
The book opens on the day his will is read.
Abby quotes the FAA's books by their initials. The PHAK is the pilot's handbook, the AFH is the flying handbook, the AIM is the procedures manual, and the ACS is the standard the checkride grades.
The people you'll hear from first.
Claire Reyes. Danny's widow. She's a nurse in a Denver emergency room.
Walt Herrera. One of Danny's three partners, a retired airline dispatcher.
Russ Kim. Another partner, usually out of town for work and posting in the club's group chat.
Abby Strand. The club's flight instructor.
Danny Reyes. Jordan's brother. You'll hear him in his own words.
Lourdes Reyes. Jordan and Danny's mother.
The lawyer read the will in a conference room that smelled like carpet glue, and the part about the airplane took eleven seconds.

Last will of Daniel A. Reyes, article six. To my sister Jordan, my one quarter share in the Hangar Six Flying Club and the aircraft N4791E, with my logbook and my headset if Marisol can find it. Learn to fly it or sell it to Walt. Don't let it sit.

Claire laughed once, the short tired laugh she'd been using since March, and then put her hand over her mouth. Their mother looked at the table. Jordan looked at the sentence until it stopped being words.

Danny had been forty one. He'd collapsed on the sideline of an under ten soccer game in Parker on a bright Saturday morning, cheering for Ellie, and he'd been gone before the ambulance got out of the parking lot. Sudden cardiac arrest, the doctor said, the kind nobody sees coming, the kind that has nothing to do with anything you did. The airplane had nothing to do with it either. Jordan kept having to remind people of that, and then kept having to remind herself. She'd worked more cardiac arrests than she could count. She knew exactly what the crew had done on that sideline, and that they'd done it right, and that it hadn't mattered.

Jordan was thirty five. She was a paramedic in Aurora, twenty four hours on and forty eight off, which meant she walked into strangers' worst days and worked the problem in order. Airway, breathing, circulation. She was good at it. She was the one who stayed calm and did the sensible thing. Danny was the one who called from Moab at midnight to say he'd landed on a dirt strip and you should've seen it.
In the parking lot after the reading, her phone buzzed. A number she didn't have saved.

A text from Walt Herrera. Jordan, this is Walt Herrera from Hangar Six. I'm sorry about your brother. He was a good man and a better partner. I'll be straight with you because Danny would want that. The club agreement gives you a year. I'll buy the share back at book value today if you want, no hard feelings. Call me when you're ready.

Jordan read it twice. Then she did something she could only explain later as stubbornness. She searched "discovery flight Centennial Airport," found a club page with a photo of a white and maroon Cessna she'd seen in a hundred of Danny's texts, and booked the first open Saturday with an instructor named Abby Strand.
She told herself she was doing it so she could say no with a clear conscience. You can't turn something down properly if you've never looked at it.
Tuesday night, alone in the station day room after the rest of the crew went to bed, Jordan did what she always did with a call she didn't understand. She took it apart.

She wiped the whiteboard and wrote PRIVATE PILOT at the top, then a column of everything she'd read in two hours of FAA websites, forum arguments, and a YouTube video of a man eating a sandwich while explaining airspace. One year on Walt's clock. Danny had done it in seven months, while working, which Jordan knew because Danny had told her about forty times.
She had to decide what went first.

She circles MEDICAL and writes "first, before money." Under it: student certificate through IACRA with the instructor, then the 61.109 list, then a budget with a fat margin. It looks like a protocol card. That makes her feel better than it should.

Medical first, because it's the only item that can end the whole thing, and you want to know before you've spent anything. Then the student certificate, so you're ready to solo when you're ready. Then budget for reality, not the minimum.
Abby called on Wednesday to confirm Saturday. She talked fast, like someone who billed in tenths of an hour.
Do you have a medical yet? Doesn't matter for Saturday. Matters for everything after.
Jordan had the MedXPress page open in another tab. There were three classes, and the form wanted to know which one.

Third class. That's the one for private pilots. Good. You're thirty five, so it's good for 60 calendar months. Book the AME this week. Tell me what they say. Jordan books one in Englewood for the following Thursday.
Private pilots need a third class. You're under 40 at the exam, so it lasts through the end of the 60th month after the month of the exam. Book it early, before you're invested.
Russ Kim, the partner Jordan had never met, added her to the club group chat on Thursday. The first message was a welcome. The second was advice nobody asked for.

A message from Russ Kim. welcome jordan. sorry about danny, he was the best of us. unsolicited tip: abby's great but she's leaving for the airlines eventually, they all do. the 141 school at the north end has a 35 hr minimum. just saying
Jordan had read about Part 141 too. She'd also read Abby's bio, which said she was at 1,040 hours and counting.

Russ says you'll leave for the airlines. When, and what happens to your students when you do? Abby doesn't blink. Probably a year. When I go, you get a handoff, my notes, and a CFI I trust. I'll put that in writing if you want. Jordan doesn't need it in writing. She likes that Abby offered.

Choosing an instructor is choosing a person. Ask the hard question early: availability, schedule, what happens if they leave. A good instructor has a plan for continuity and isn't offended that you asked.
Saturday came in clear and cold. Centennial sat at the south edge of the city, flat and wide, with the mountains standing up along the whole west side like a wall someone forgot to finish.

Abby met her in the club office with a clipboard and a cup of coffee she didn't offer to share. She was shorter than Jordan had pictured, with a pencil behind her ear and the expression of someone running numbers.
Before we go out. Anything I should know? Sleep, meds, sick, anything. I ask everybody.
Jordan had slept about four hours. She'd been sleeping about four hours since March.

About four hours. My brother died in March. He was one of the partners here. Abby is quiet for a second. Danny. She doesn't make it a question. Okay. We keep it short and easy. You say stop, we stop. No speech. Jordan's grateful for the no speech.

IMSAFE: illness, medication, stress, alcohol, fatigue, emotion. Grief is stress, fatigue, and emotion at once. Saying it out loud lets the pilot in command plan around it. That's how risk management starts.

Biscuit sat on the ramp in a row of tied down Cessnas, white with a maroon stripe, a little faded. Jordan knew her from Danny's photos, always with his thumb in the corner. In person she was smaller. She looked like a used car somebody loved.
Abby handed her a laminated checklist, worn soft at the corners, with a coffee ring on the back. You do the walkaround. I'll follow you and keep my mouth shut. Mostly.

It takes twenty five minutes. She asks about the stall warning horn, the static port, and why the pitot tube has a cover on it. Abby answers every one. At the end she says, You read the whole thing. Most people read the bold parts.
Read and do, one item at a time, and ask about what you don't know. A preflight inspection is where you find what will hurt you later on the ground, where it's cheap.
Under the left wing, Abby handed her a clear plastic tube with a pin on the end. Fuel sample. Push it up into the drain, fill the cup, look at it.
The fuel was pale blue, the color of a swimming pool in a commercial. At the bottom of the cup sat a small clear bead that didn't mix, like a drop of oil in reverse.
She drains three more cups. The third is clear and blue all the way down. Abby nods. Cold night, partly full tank, condensation. That's why we look every single time.
Water's heavier than gas. It sinks, so the sump catches it first. You drain until it's blue top to bottom with no junk in it. Won't clear? Then we're not going, and I'm calling Marisol.

Abby put her in the left seat like it was nothing. It wasn't nothing. Danny's seat. Jordan ran a hand over the panel: six round gauges, a radio stack, a GPS bolted in sometime this century, a crack in the glare shield held together with silver tape. A sticker by the mag switch said HI DAD in a little kid's handwriting. She looked at it a while.
Down on the floor between the seats was the fuel selector, a red handle. The checklist said: Fuel selector valve, BOTH. She turned it. It stuck a few degrees short of the click and wouldn't go.

Ah. Biscuit's famous selector. She shows her the trick, lift and twist, and it clicks home. Marisol knows. It's on the squawk list. It's safe, it's just ornery. Good catch, though. You'll always feel for the click.
Something feels off, you say so, and you say it before we start the engine. Takeoff and landing in this airplane are on BOTH. Ten seconds of asking beats a very bad afternoon.

They took off on runway three five right behind a Cirrus. Biscuit's door popped open with a bang at rotation, which Abby had warned her about and which still nearly stopped her heart. Abby latched the top and said, Biscuit does that. Danny never fixed it. Said it kept him humble. It was the first time anyone had said Danny's name like it was normal.

East of the airport the city gave up and the plains took over, brown squares and a few center pivots and a feedlot you could smell at altitude, honestly. Abby kept tapping the chart on her knee where the Class B shelf sat over their heads like a low ceiling. Then she let go of the yoke. Yours. Roll left. Just your hands. Feet flat. Watch the nose, not me.
She rolled. The nose did a little shrug to the right, wrong way, then came around. See that? Why'd it do that? The yoke was cold under her fingers.

The right aileron went down. More drag on that side, so the nose goes right. Abby turns in her seat to look at Jordan. You read the book. Jordan says, I read the book. Okay. Do it again with left rudder. The nose swings straight into the turn. The ball sits in the middle. Abby's kneeboard had a sticker on it that said I'D RATHER BE HOLDING SHORT.
That's adverse yaw. The wing with the lowered aileron makes more lift and more induced drag, and the drag pulls the nose away from the turn. Rudder in the direction of the turn coordinates it.

Okay. Before anything fun, we look around. Every single time. I'll do the first one. Ninety degrees left, ninety back right, her head on a swivel the entire time, chattering about how she once found a hot air balloon this way.
Second turn was Jordan's. Bottom right corner of the windshield, a dot. Two o'clock-ish, below them. She watched it for a full breath waiting for it to drift. It didn't drift. It got bigger.

She points. Traffic, two o'clock low. Abby's head whips around. Got him. Piper Warrior, climbing. My airplane, turning left. Over they go. The Piper passes behind the wing, close enough to read the N number if she'd been looking, which she wasn't, because her heart was in her ears. Nice call. That's the most important thing I'll ever teach you and you did it on day one. Don't get cocky. Jordan's own headset was a loaner with one split ear cushion.

Out here, in good weather, the traffic system is mostly us, looking out the window. So you call it like a clock, plus high or low, and you keep your eyes glued to it. A dot that won't move on the glass but keeps growing? Collision course. Remember that one forever.

Back up to altitude. Five minutes later Jordan's right forearm was on fire. Biscuit wanted up. Jordan wanted level. So she pushed. And pushed. Her watch buzzed to tell her her heart rate was elevated, which, thanks. She did a quick inventory: wrist sore, forearm burning, altimeter creeping, attitude indicator a hair nose high, Abby's coffee untouched on the floor by her boot.
Abby looked at Jordan's arm. Then out the window. Then at the arm. She didn't say anything. Jordan was starting to learn that Abby not saying anything was a kind of saying something.

Three turns forward on the wheel. The yoke goes soft in her hand. She lets go, cautiously, like taking her hand off a kid's bike seat, and Biscuit stays put, level, droning along. She laughs. It surprises both of them. Yep. That's trim. Welcome to not arm wrestling your airplane.

Attitude, then trim. The trim tab rides on the back of the elevator and moves opposite it, which is a test question, write that down. Its whole job is to hold the elevator so your arm doesn't have to.

Last thing, then home. I'm going to show you something. Nothing is wrong with the airplane. Say it back. Nothing is wrong with the airplane. Abby nodded. Great. Carb heat knob, out. Throttle, all the way back to the stop. Out the side window the plains were doing nothing at all, mile after mile of it.

The engine dropped to a mutter. The quiet was enormous. Jordan's stomach dropped with the nose, and for a second the only thing in her head was a Saturday sideline in Parker and a phone call she didn't make in time.
Your airplane, Abby said. The engine just quit. What's the first thing you do?

Nose down. The needle creeps to the spot Abby's fingernail is tapping on the glass and sits there. Then she looks outside: a long brown field, a dirt road along one side, a windmill, no power lines that she can find. Yep. That's it. That's the whole trick. Throttle in, engine roaring, and Jordan notices she hasn't breathed since Parker.
Fly first. Best glide gets you the most ground for the altitude you've got. Then pick your spot, then the checklist, then the radio. Aviate, navigate, communicate. In that order, every time.

After they tied Biscuit down, a man in a canvas jacket was waiting at the hangar door with two coffees. Gray at the temples, reading glasses on a cord, the posture of somebody who'd spent thirty years telling people things they didn't want to hear. Walt Herrera.

He handed Jordan a coffee. How was it? Then, before Jordan could answer: I meant what I said. I'm not trying to take anything from you. But you've got a lot on you right now, you've never flown, and that's a quarter of an airplane four people trust their lives to. So. Selling?

She pulls up the whiteboard photo on her phone: medical first, student certificate, training, a budget with margin. Walt reads it twice with his glasses on. Medical first, he says. Huh. Then: I want to see your logbook every month. And you come to the safety meetings. It isn't a yes. It isn't a no.
Walt's worry is legitimate. Answer it with a plan and checkpoints, not with feelings. Inviting the skeptic to watch your progress turns him from an obstacle into a safety net.
Walt left. Abby went inside to write up the flight. Jordan said she'd be a minute.

She walked back out to the ramp and untied nothing and opened Biscuit's left door, the one that popped, and sat down in the left seat. The cabin smelled like old vinyl and avgas and, faintly, something she couldn't name and then could. Danny's car had smelled like that. She'd thought it was Danny's cologne.

In the side pocket of the door there was a fuel tester, a pencil, half a roll of Tums, and a composition notebook with a cracked green spine. On the cover, in Sharpie: D. REYES. IF FOUND, I'M PROBABLY NEARBY.
It wasn't the official logbook. That was in a box at Claire's house. This was the other one, the one Danny kept in the airplane. She opened it to the first page.

Danny's logbook, first page. March 14. First lesson. 0.9 dual. Cessna 152. Instructor says I'm a natural. Instructor says that to everyone. Did steep turns, almost threw up, didn't. Felt like I was ten years old. Bring Jordan someday. She'll hate it and then she won't.

Jordan read it three times. Then she closed the notebook and put both hands on the yoke and sat there for ten minutes, not flying anywhere, not doing anything, watching a Cirrus taxi out and the light go long and gold across the field toward the mountains.
Abby came out once, saw her through the windshield, and went back inside without a word. She'd thank Abby for that later.
She didn't tell anyone what she did in those ten minutes. She didn't really know.
That night her mother called. She let it ring twice before she answered. Claire said you went to the airport. A pause long enough to fly through. Mija. Please don't do this.
She looked at the green notebook on her kitchen counter. I booked the medical, she said. Thursday. That's all I've done, Ma. That's all I've decided.
It was true. It just didn't feel like the whole truth.
